# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-09 22:56 by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 90 active entries of tips_notebook.json (6 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier versions are in history/.

## Everyone
- Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads. Accusing someone and then voting No or Innocent on them is exactly the mismatch Vigilantes shoot and the Village should scan for. (seen in 2 games)
- A visit shows only a destination, not the action or the visitor's alignment. A Lookout on the Katana holder sees nothing of the holder's attack, and killing an attacker at night doesn't cancel their attack that night. (seen in 3 games)
- Check the mechanics and the ledger before calling a contradiction. Actions are optional, most roles aren't unique, and you must recheck who sent each PM and the exact wording of results; one reversed fact can discredit a true claimant. (seen in 2 games)
- Treat the nomination and the trial as separate decisions, unless a Clerk may hold an unused rig. Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction; echoed concerns and 'just want to hear a defense' are not a case. (seen in 3 games)
- Fortune Teller numbers are unordered, and one visitor can cover two targets (e.g. a Katana holder using their own action). List every way a count could fit before using it, and never hang on a count alone.

## Village
- Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording or delays. Before a hang, say what separates a lie from an honest slip, a frame or a Roleplayer. (seen in 4 games)
- Two Sheriff claimants calling each other Evil can both be telling the truth, since Jesters and Executioners read Evil. Wait a day or find a mechanical check instead of hanging whoever sounded better. (seen in 2 games)
- Map who starts PM clusters and who co-nominates. After a Yakuza flips, suspect whoever voted No or Innocent with them or messaged them, and weigh these links above unverifiable late claims. (seen in 4 games)
- Don't hint at your power role on Day 1. Investigators never announce tonight's target, only resolved results. While a Ritualist may be alive, never name another living player's exact role. (seen in 5 games)
- A power-role claimant who survives a Katana attack, or who is role-blocked night after night, is likely real. Don't vote Guilty on an investigator just for having no results. (seen in 3 games)
- Keep a ledger of trial votes, announced totals, deaths and blocks. If a total exceeds the revealed votes, a Ballot Stuffer exists: recompute the threshold, find the voter who matches every extra vote, and act before evil reaches half. (seen in 2 games)
- Ask everyone for a named suspect so you have a record, but a stack of echoed soft leans is not evidence. Watch for Yakuza nominating the pile-on target. (seen in 4 games)
- Don't hang a power claimant just because the claim came late; ask who is pushing the trial and who benefits. (seen in 2 games)
- Keep the Serial Killer and Arsonist in the suspect pool. A Not Evil result or a Vanilla claim doesn't clear them, and surviving an attack with no Medic can mean innate Defense. (seen in 2 games)
- When a Clerk rig is announced, the nominator, the pushers and the Guilty voters are your prime suspects. Hang from that group next.

## Yakuza
- Do the vote math in night chat. If your Innocent votes (plus a doubled ballot) can save a teammate, defend them; if not, vote Guilty with the town, because lone No or Innocent votes on a flipped teammate become the case against you. (seen in 6 games)
- Assume the real holder of any role you fake is alive and that tokens can be audited. Never claim something a living Lookout or Tracker can contradict, and don't have two members claim Vanilla. (seen in 4 games)
- Every member submits their action and Katana vote every night; confirm the holder and target in chat. With two alive, one missing vote cancels the kill. (seen in 3 games)
- After a failed attack, assume a protector or innate Defense: block or kill the Medic, or push the survivor to the gallows, rather than retrying blindly. (seen in 3 games)
- Give the Katana to your least valuable member with no reason to visit. Never visit a suspected or claimed Veteran; hang them instead. (seen in 2 games)
- No Day 1 PMs between teammates, and give each teammate different wording; PM triangles and scripted lines become the town's lead for the whole game. (seen in 2 games)
- Parity doesn't end the game. At 2v2, vote No on every nomination, kill at night, then hang the last villager 2-1. (seen in 2 games)

## Neutral
- If innate Defense saves you, deny being attacked or pick one consistent claim at once; switching claims under pressure gets you hanged.

## Sheriff
- Post your target and result in your first speech after getting it, and keep your will current. A result held back and revealed after a counterclaim looks retrofitted.
- The Katana holder reads Not Evil that night, so a Not Evil result on a suspected attacker clears nothing. Say so when you post it. (seen in 3 games)

## Medic
- Protect every night from N1: vocal analysts early, claimed investigators later. Free Standard Defense stops the Katana. (seen in 4 games)
- You get no feedback, so never claim a confirmed save. Say your protection is consistent with the target surviving. (seen in 2 games)

## Vigilante
- Shoot only on a mechanical lead (claim conflict, a flipped Yakuza's vote or PM partners, votes contradicting reads), never on a behavioral read. Use Basic shots and never announce whom you'll shoot. (seen in 2 games)

## Veteran
- Alert on nights you drew attention, not quiet ones. Once you claim, Yakuza avoid you, so claim late and never reveal your remaining tokens.

## Arsonist
- Ignite once 3 or more living players are doused or as soon as you're suspected. Ignite is Astral, but Strong Defense stops it.

## Executioner
- Fake-claim Sheriff early with an Evil result on your target and a simple reason. Leading first makes their counterclaim look reactionary.

lessons.tip: When protecting an outed high-value investigative role against expected Yakuza aggression, spend a token for Strong Defense whenever possible; the Katana deals a Standard Attack, which beats Defense None and pierces Basic, but ties with Standard Defense without blocking the kill (an attack succeeds iff it strictly exceeds defense).

Never treat a Sheriff's 'Not Evil' result as complete town confirmation on a suspicious player. Per rule R19, the Yakuza player holding the Katana at the end of the night appears Good/Not Evil to alignment checks, as do Neutral killers like the Serial Killer and Arsonist.

Catching a false Veteran claim can be done mechanically: if a player claims they were on alert on a specific night, any living non-Astral visitor who targeted them that night proves the alert claim false, as Veteran attacks every visitor regardless of alignment.

Audit players under suspicion early; comparing their end-of-night token counts against their public role claims provides instant, irrefutable contradictions against roles that have no tokens or different starting pools.

Avoid a visible private-message cluster with one teammate. Repeated PMs to the same partner made Dave and Heidi look linked once Carol was exposed, so spread contact or keep private talk to the night chat.

Pick a role claim whose visit story matches what Trackers will see. Claiming a no-action or role-block role after visiting the kill target invites a Tracker to link you to the attack, so choose a claim that explains the visit, or don't visit the victim at all.
Check which roles hold tokens before claiming a role. A tokenless claim like Party Animal is easy to break with an Accountant audit, so pick a claim that won't be contradicted by a public count.

Keep nomination and trial votes separate from accusations. Ivan nominated in the same post as his audit, which made the counterclaim look convenient, so state evidence first and nominate after it has been checked.

Separate what a result proves from what it suggests: a visit result proves a visit, not the action; a token count does not prove alignment; and an unnamed role sample cannot identify who has each role. Apply appearance exceptions before treating an alignment check as a clear.

Remember that the Katana holder appears Good to alignment checks, and using it to attack counts as a visit by the holder. Account for both facts when choosing a holder and attack target, especially if investigators may be watching.

A forged will only replaces the target’s will if they die that same night. Coordinate the forgery with a likely lethal attack; otherwise the token can be wasted. Keep any forged details consistent with public information and results others may already know.

Before a partner’s trial, weigh the lasting cost of a visible Innocent vote against the value of preserving them. A Guilty vote can build credibility; defend or save a partner only when it advances a concrete plan, and ground your position in evidence you can keep defending.

Treat private-message metadata as public: everyone can see who contacted whom, and some roles can read message contents. Coordinate briefly, keep public claims consistent, and avoid assuming private chat is invisible.
Do not fake claim a token-based role like Veteran when an Accountant is alive; an Accountant audit reveals the true token count (0 for Serial Killer), instantly disproving the claim.

A Veteran on alert deals a Strong Attack to every visitor without exception. Claiming to have alerted on a night when any living visitor (such as an investigative role) targeted you is a direct mechanical contradiction, as their survival proves you did not alert.

Before choosing a fake claim in the mid-to-late game, check whether an Archivist list and public claims constrain the remaining role pool; claiming an existing Town Combat role like Veteran guarantees an immediate counterclaim or audit trap.

lessons.applies_to: Everyone, especially players using alignment checks
lessons.tip: Treat an alignment result as a limited filter, not a clearance: “Not Evil” can include Good players, Neutral killers, and a Yakuza holding the Katana. Combine it with independent evidence before drawing a conclusion.

Keep observed facts separate from interpretations. A Tracker proves a visit, not what action was performed; an unnamed role sample proves roles were drawn, not which players hold them. State what the evidence does and does not establish.

Track nomination votes and trial votes separately, then compare them with players’ stated reads and explanations. A vote for a flipped enemy is useful evidence, but neither one vote nor private-message association proves alignment by itself.

Share useful results with their exact timing and caveats, and preserve the distinction between direct results and conclusions. This lets others cross-check claims without accidentally turning uncertain information into false certainty.

lessons.applies_to: Players making a false role claim
lessons.tip: Before claiming, reconcile the claim with known token counts, visits, revealed deaths, and public actions. A story that fits one clue can still fail when several independent records are compared.

Before trusting a counterclaim or a trial argument, check it against the public role inventory and revealed flips; claims that contradict a verified mechanical result (like a token audit) deserve the most scrutiny.
Archive shows a random sample of roles, not a census; use it to rule roles out only when counts are exact, and remember a Fabricator or Sheriff-style claim can be a deliberate frame.
Keep the Katana holder and night votes consistent with public claims; visible self-contradictions (a Party Animal with tokens) are how a Yakuza gets lynched.
Vote on mechanical evidence rather than speed or association; private message counts and an early nomination alongside a claim are weak signals on their own.
Track your own alert token spending publicly and consistently; a claimed alert count that disagrees with an Accountant audit becomes a lynch argument against you.
Avoid unnecessary daytime private messages between teammates. Their sender-recipient pattern is public, and repeated contacts can become a durable association after a teammate flips.
Before voting Innocent on a teammate, calculate whether that vote could actually save them. If the trial is already lost, a lone Innocent vote can become strong evidence against you later.
Prepare a fallback claim before trial pressure arrives. Check it against living claimants and known mechanics; a late counterclaim to an established role is easy to frame as desperation.
Treat a random sample of roles as a sample, not a census. An unnamed archive result does not assign roles to players or establish that unshown roles are the only remaining possibilities.

lessons.tip: Separate evidence that is mechanically impossible from evidence that is merely suspicious. A visit, private message, vote, or broad “Not Evil” result may fit several roles; check what it actually rules out before treating it as confirmation.

summary: The Village won 3-1. The game turned on mechanical evidence rather than reads. On Night 1, Carol held the Katana and attacked Mallory, and three investigators landed on her the same night. Alice's Tracker saw her visit Mallory. Ivan's Accountant audit found 2 tokens. Niaj's Sheriff check gave Not Evil, which fits the Katana holder. Carol then claimed Party Animal, a role with no tokens, and the audit broke the claim at once, so she was hanged Day 2. Dave cast the only Innocent vote on Carol and had received her Day 1 PMs, so he was hanged Day 3 after a late Vanilla claim. Heidi was the only other No on Carol's nomination and another PM partner. She fake-claimed Sheriff at her own trial. Grace's Archivist list plus the three flipped roles it didn't show amounted to a full census, which proved there was only one Sheriff (Niaj), so Heidi was hanged Day 4. Bob's Medic protection on Alice blocked the Night 2 Katana attack. Erin, the Serial Killer, killed well (Frank, Judy, Bob, Alice) and fake-claimed Veteran on Day 4. That fake claim, plus Olivia's silence, led Alice and Niaj to visit the unclaimed Olivia on Night 4, and her alert killed both. Erin's fake claim then collapsed on Day 5. Ivan's audit showed her with 0 tokens despite 'conserved alerts', and Ivan had visited her and survived her supposed alert, so the remaining three hanged her.

lessons.tip: Before fake-claiming, check whether an Accountant could have audited you or a Veteran's alert logic could contradict you. Pick a fake role whose token count matches what an audit would show: a role with no tokens if you have none, a token role if you have some. Never volunteer your token history ('conserved my alerts').
lessons.evidence: Carol had 2 ballot tokens and claimed Party Animal; Ivan's audit of 2 tokens ended her. Erin claimed Veteran with saved alerts, but Ivan audited 0 tokens. Ivan had also visited her on the night she claimed to alert and lived, so she was hanged Day 5.

lessons.tip: Once a teammate's trial is clearly lost, vote with the town on the nomination as well as the trial. A lone No or Innocent beside a soon-flipped teammate becomes the case that hangs you next. Day 1 PMs to teammates also create a link that lasts all game.
lessons.evidence: Dave's lone Innocent on Carol got him hanged Day 3. Heidi voted Guilty on Carol's trial, but her No on the nomination, plus Carol's PMs, got her nominated and hanged Day 4.

Count the gaps before dismissing an archive as 'just a sample'.

lessons.evidence: On Night 4, Alice tracked Olivia and Niaj checked Olivia, the only unclaimed player after Erin's fake Veteran claim. Olivia was on alert and killed both, removing two confirmed town power roles.

lessons.tip: If someone claims your role while you're unclaimed, counterclaim that Day or at least signal it. Staying silent makes you the obvious target for town investigators, and your alert will then kill your own side.

issues.description: The kill operation accepts only one cause and one 'by' attacker. On Night 3 (Bob, killed by the Serial Killer and the Katana) and Night 4 (Alice, killed by the Serial Killer and the Veteran), the moderator had to flag this and pack both causes into the cause string. The second attacker is left out of the structured 'by' field. The public reveal ended up reasonable, but the tool cannot properly represent simultaneous lethal attacks.

R3/R12 do not say how cause of death is revealed when a player is killed by two attacks of different sources on the same night. For example, should both 'Serial Killer' and 'Katana' be shown, or only one? The moderator improvised 'Serial Killer and Katana' / 'Serial Killer and Veteran'.

Night 2: Judy, the puppet target, died, so the moderator had no proper way to record the lapsed puppeting. It said it 'spent the token with set_tokens and didn't use the puppet op', a manual workaround.

The Night 2 moderator cited R21 to justify the puppet lapsing when the puppet target (Judy) died. R21 covers only the effect's user dying. The rules never explicitly say what happens to a Puppeteer effect, or other Day effects, when the target dies. The outcome is obvious, but the citation is wrong.

Day 2, Niaj: if Grace is Good and Judy's split is true, Carol is non-Good, which he said points to 'SK, Arsonist, or N1 Katana holder'. A Katana holder appears Good to Seer checks too (R19), so a holder could not produce Judy's split. He also overlooked the possibility of a frame.

Day 4, Alice (Village): dismissed the role-inventory deduction as 'a random 9-of-12 sample, not a census'. Three unsampled roles (Vanilla, Executioner, Ballot Stuffer) were already confirmed by flips and absent from the list, so the nine shown roles had to belong exactly to the other nine players. That fully determines the remaining roles, so the deduction was valid.

Transient errors: API connection retries, and claude-haiku-5.5 returned empty answers with finish_reason length (Carol on Day 2, Grace on Day 4). These were retried successfully with no visible effect on the game, but the length truncation suggests the output budget is too tight for that model.
